topic: A/B test of a new checkout page
decision: whether to roll out the new one-page checkout to all customers

columns.variant: control = old checkout, new_checkout = new one-page checkout
columns.conversion_pct: orders as a percentage of sessions
columns.median_page_load_s: median checkout page load time, seconds

findings.text: Average order value is about the same in both versions ($413 old, $411 new).
On mobile, conversion fell from 2.09% with the old checkout to 1.65% with the new one. On desktop it rose from 3.15% to 3.58%.
Sessions were split evenly between the versions (50.0% old, 50.0% new), as designed.
Tablet conversion rose from 2.35% to 2.92%, but tablets are only 3% of sessions.
Mobile is 68% of sessions, so over the 14 days the new checkout produced 6.5% fewer orders in total (4,838 against 5,177).
More visitors started the new checkout (+5.3% checkouts started).
The new checkout loads faster on desktop (median 1.9 s against 2.4 s).

A bug that hid the payment button on some phones in the new checkout was fixed on 26 September. Mobile conversion on the new checkout was 2.24% on 26 and 27 September, close to the old checkout, but two days is too short to judge.
Conversion is highest on Saturdays in both versions.
Both versions dipped on 20 September during a payment-provider outage.

main.gist: The new checkout loses mobile conversions and lowers total orders

caveat.gist: A mobile payment-button bug was fixed on 26 September

facts.q: What was the mobile conversion rate with the old checkout and with the new checkout, in percent?
By how many percent did total orders change with the new checkout compared with the old one? Use a negative number for a fall.
